extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations, especially government/public affairs officers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for government public affairs (public relations) work — its goals, practitioner competencies, communication models, tools (including e-gov and broadcasting), media relations tactics, internal information management, and barriers to effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informing constituents
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary job of government public affairs practitioners is to inform. Ensuring the constant flow of information to persons outside and inside government is generally the top priority; these activities are accomplished through external, internal, and media-specific information services and are predicated on informing and educating the public, not lobbying for a desired outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information functions can be global; public affairs should deliver up-to-date and accurate information. Examples include departmental information products and web services (see Figure 16.1). Exception: when targeting overseas audiences information may intentionally influence. Avoid substituting information delivery for lobbying; focus on accuracy and timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensuring active cooperation in government programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use communication campaigns to expand citizens' knowledge about civic obligations and to encourage actions that fulfill them (e.g., voting, curbside recycling, compliance with regulations like mandatory seat-belt use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campaigns should explain why compliance matters and what actions citizens should take; they address questions such as how citizens learn about obligations and what changes in regulations are forthcoming. Examples include immunization drives and tax-filing reminders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fostering citizen support for established policies and programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use public affairs to build citizen understanding and support for policies and programs (e.g., census participation, neighborhood crime watch, disaster relief, public health campaigns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectives vary by agency, but communications should promote understanding and participation; straightforward messaging is emphasized. Communications affect people’s control over government and must be integrated with planning, budgeting, and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serving as the public’s advocate to government administrators
rubrics_metrics.description: Public affairs officers act as a bridge, conveying public opinion and values to decision makers, managing public issues within the organization, and encouraging public accessibility to administration officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should maintain polling and community contacts, bring well-researched arguments to management when public sentiment requires policy review (example: TSA/screening modifications), and balance communicating organizational agendas with communicating public desires back to officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing information internally
rubrics_metrics.description: Facilitate and advance management’s messages inside the organization; ensure all echelons are conversant with issues to prevent destructive rumors and enable consistent public responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain knowledgeable frontline staff (reception/greeters), ensure employees are apprised of organizational developments, and provide internal information services so staff can respond accurately to public inquiries. Speed and accuracy are critical because statements are disseminated instantly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitating media relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain relationships with local and national media; serve as the organization’s conduit for media inquiries and educate journalists on the organization, its practices, and its policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide timely and accurate information, use hotlines and dedicated clearinghouses (examples: FSIS hotline, Department of Defense’s DDI) to meet media expectations for immediacy and to encourage balanced reporting. Early sharing of information promotes better-informed journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building community and nation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use public affairs and national campaigns to promote community development, public health, social programs, interethnic relations, international investment, job skills, and other nation-building objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ multiple channels (PSAs, events, partnerships with faith-based and nonprofit groups) and tailor programs to community needs (examples: USDA nutrition icons, national HIV-prevention campaigns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public affairs practitioner competencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must possess a solid mix of communication skills linked to a comprehensive understanding of the organization’s culture, policies, practices, and constituents and should be integral members of the executive management team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competencies include writing op-eds, producing infomercials, handling media relations, and advising management under statutory constraints; practitioners should combine communication skills with subject-matter understanding to inform and influence appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication models and mixed-motive approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Government communicators operate primarily in the public information model but may also use two-way symmetrical models; often a mixed-motive approach is used to balance organizational interests and stakeholder needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use research to advise internal change when appropriate (example: Department of Transportation/TSA case), but remain transparent and objective. Be aware of model limitations and choose the approach that best balances informing, advocacy, and stakeholder engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic government (e-gov) objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Use information and communication technologies to deliver services and encourage citizen participation — deliver web-based information on demand, improve public access to services, and respond quickly/accurately to information requests (including FOIA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E-gov should expand access (example: NSF grant and announcement services), support on-demand delivery of products/records/data, and harness technology to increase transparency and citizen engagement. Sweden’s national policy and U.S. agency e-gov initiatives are cited as models.

rubrics_metrics.name: International broadcasting and public diplomacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage, inform, and influence overseas audiences about national policies, principles, and values to provide context, set agenda, forge consensus, and shape preferences of international actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use speaker programs, Internet, host-nation media, public events, films, exhibits, and cultural/educational exchanges (examples: Voice of America, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, Alhurra). Maintain professional independence while coordinating policy guidance at senior levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionable credibility (barrier)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived lack of believability and trustworthiness in government communications undermines public affairs; accusations of 'just PR' or propaganda damage credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigate credibility issues through transparency and legal/administrative measures (examples: Electronic FOIA Amendments of 1996, Data Quality Act of 2001), ensure accuracy and objectivity of disseminated information, and avoid contradictory or shifting messages that erode trust (cited WMD intelligence example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public apathy (barrier)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apathy and lack of citizen interest make it difficult for government to reach and mobilize broad publics; many citizens may not engage with government processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design campaigns and participation mechanisms to lower barriers to involvement; acknowledge structural complexity and perceptions of impotence that reduce turnout at hearings and advisory processes. Tailor outreach to broaden appeal and lower effort required for participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative hostility (barrier)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congressional and legislative opposition to information activities can constrain public affairs functions and reduce practitioner effectiveness or status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of historical and political sensitivities about public-sector communications; maintain compliance with statutes and cost/record-keeping rules (example: FACA requirements for advisory groups) and build legitimacy by ensuring advice is relevant, objective, timely, and cost-conscious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soliciting and motivating citizen involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Public affairs officers are responsible for actively soliciting and motivating citizens to participate in decision-making processes (e.g., required community engagement for major infrastructure in some countries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use legal mechanisms (FACA) and best practices from other nations (Australia’s laws requiring citizen input, policies in Finland/Netherlands/Spain) to structure inclusive participation; anticipate internal resistance from officials who fear altered plans and manage trade-offs between expertise and public input.
